hits.hook: ★ 202K: 2,000 years of height data as the nutrition survey committees cannot fudge.
hits.text:
50 BC: the tallest men a Roman legion ever faced were the Germans and the Celts, and they lived on the herd. Caesar wrote it down through gritted teeth.

800: the tallest people in Europe were the Norse, and they lived on butter, cheese, fish and salt meat.

1850: the tallest people on earth were the Cheyenne and the Sioux, and they lived on bison.

1899: the shortest men in the British army came out of the mill towns, and they lived on bread, tea and jam.

1954: the shortest people in the developed world were the Japanese. Milk went into every school lunch that year and they grew 10cm inside a generation.

2000: the two Koreas shared a language, a border and a set of grandparents, and the south, on beef and eggs, stood up to 8cm above the north, on rice.

2026: the tallest people on earth are the Dutch, and they drink more milk per head than any nation alive.

Height is the only nutrition survey that cannot be funded, fudged or reworded by a committee.

It is taken against a wall, in front of a mother, and it has returned the same verdict on every continent for 2,000 years.

The tall ones had the herd. The short ones had the field.
hits.draft_en:
Height is the nutrition survey that cannot be funded, fudged, or reworded.

Caesar’s Germans and Celts lived on the herd. Norse on butter, cheese, fish, salt meat. Cheyenne and Sioux on bison. Mill-town Britain on bread, tea, and jam, and the shortest soldiers came out of those towns.

Japan put milk in school lunches in 1954 and grew about 10 cm in a generation. South Korea on beef and eggs stands roughly 8 cm over the North on rice. The Dutch lead the planet and drink more milk per head than anyone.

Taken against a wall, in front of a mother, for 2,000 years: the tall ones had the herd. The short ones had the field.

Before you rewrite human diet again, measure the kids.
hits.video_tip: 22s timeline cards: Rome → Norse → Plains → mill towns → Japan milk → Koreas → Dutch. End card: “Height cannot be fudged.”

hits.hook: ★ 172K: Irish booleying outlawed because living on milk without a master worked.
hits.text:
For 300 years the English government in Ireland tried to make it illegal for an Irish family to spend the summer with its cows.

The practice was called booleying. Every May the household left the winter village and walked the herd up into the hills, to a cluster of huts on the summer pasture, and lived there until October. Grandparents, children, the lot. The men came and went. The women ran the booley, and the booley ran on milk: fresh, soured, curdled, buttered, and eaten as the day's meals. The grass was free because it was up a mountain, and a family that owned 8 cows and a mountain wanted for nothing until the frost.

The English could not stand it. A people that walked away every summer could not be counted, tithed or made to plough. The Statute of Kilkenny, 1366, forbade the Irish to booley their cattle on any land held by the English, and licensed the English to seize the herd if they did. By 1612 the King's attorney general in Dublin could report that it had been made penal for an Englishman even to allow it.

Edmund Spenser, who had been handed 3,000 acres of confiscated Cork, wrote a whole pamphlet on what was wrong with Ireland, and this was near the top of it. Living out with the herd, he said, taught the Irish to be wild and to feed themselves without a master.

That was the objection, in his own words. Booleying was outlawed because it worked.

The remedy, over the next century, was to take the hills, fence the grass, put the family on a rented acre in the valley, and hand it a potato.

The last booleys in Ireland were still walked up the hills of Achill in the 1940s, by people who had been told for 600 years that their summers were a crime.
hits.draft_en:
For 300 years English rule tried to make it illegal for an Irish family to spend summer with its cows.

Booleying: walk the herd into the hills each May, live on fresh, soured, curdled milk and butter until October. Free grass. Eight cows and a mountain, and the household wanted for little until frost.

That was the problem. A people who fed themselves without a master could not be counted, tithed, or forced to plough. Spenser said living out with the herd taught the Irish to be wild.

The “remedy” was fences, a rented acre, and a potato.

When a food system is outlawed because it works, ask who the next chart is for.
hits.video_tip: 20s: herd walking hills → milk bowls → statute text overlay → potato handoff. Punchline: “Outlawed because it worked.”

hits.text:

- Population: about 390,000
- World's Strongest Man titles: 9
- Jón Páll Sigmarsson: 4
- Magnús Ver Magnússon: 4

hits.hook: ★ 47K: Elizabeth I’s black teeth as Britain’s first recorded sugar casualty.
hits.text:
1598. A German visitor at Greenwich watches the Queen of England go past and writes it all down. The pearls in her ears. The false red hair. The small crown. The stately air, the mild voice, the six languages. And her teeth, black, a defect he says the English seem subject to from their too great use of sugar.

Elizabeth I is 65, the richest woman in Europe, and her mouth is the first sugar casualty in Britain anyone bothered to record.

Sugar arrived then by the loaf from Madeira, the Canaries and Brazil, priced like a spice and sold by the apothecary as medicine. The rich ate it to prove they could. She was served entire banquets of it: castles, ships, chessboards, marzipan fruit built to look like the orchard, all of it admired and then eaten. Every ambassador who met her went home and mentioned the teeth.

The poor could not afford the stuff. They kept their teeth and were pitied for it.

Four centuries on the price ran the other way, and the rot ran down the ladder with it. A queen's mouth is now the cheapest thing in the shop.
hits.draft_en:
In 1598 a German visitor wrote down Queen Elizabeth’s black teeth and blamed English sugar.

She was 65, the richest woman in Europe, and sugar still cost like a spice. Banquets of sugar castles and marzipan fruit. Ambassadors went home talking about her mouth.

The poor could not afford the rot. They kept their teeth and were pitied for it.

Four centuries later the price flipped. A queen’s mouth is now the cheapest thing in the shop.

Status foods become mass foods. Pathology follows the price.
hits.video_tip: 18s: 1598 court → sugar loaf → black teeth card → modern candy aisle. End: “rot ran down the ladder.”

hits.hook: ★ 38K: Butter would need to stop being butter to clog arteries the seed-oil way.
hits.text:

For butter to clog your arteries, it would have to carry linoleic acid. It brings about 2%.

For butter to clog your arteries, it would have to oxidise the particle carrying your cholesterol. That reaction needs polyunsaturated fat, the kind butter barely contains.

For butter to clog your arteries, it would have to bring sugar to glycate that particle. It brings none worth weighing.

For butter to clog your arteries, it would have to be new. People churned it for thousands of years before heart disease became the leading cause of death.

For butter to clog your arteries, Americans would have had to eat more of it as heart disease climbed. They were eating less of it every decade.

Every rung needs butter to stop being butter.

It would need linoleic acid. It brings about 2%.

hits.hook: ★ 23K: Plains tribes tallest in 1890s; flour rations → highest diabetes rates.
hits.text:
The Plains tribes were the tallest people on earth in the 1890s, and one generation of government rations took it all away.

The Plains man of the 1890s:
- Height: 172.6cm, tallest in the world
- Europeans: several centimetres shorter
- Diet: buffalo hump, tongue, marrow and liver
- Winter food: pemmican, dried meat pounded into fat
- Buffalo: tens of millions

The Plains man of the reservation:
- Buffalo left in 1889: 1,091
- Diet: government flour, sugar, coffee and bacon
- 1889: Congress cuts the beef ration
- 1890: Wounded Knee
- 20th century: commodity flour, shortening and processed cheese

Their descendants today:
- Diabetes: highest of any racial group in America
- Rate: more than twice that of white Americans

Same people. Same land. Same sky.

The buffalo went, the flour came, and the tallest people on earth became the most diabetic people in their own country.
hits.draft_en:
In the 1890s Plains men averaged 172.6 cm, among the tallest on earth, on buffalo hump, tongue, marrow, liver, and pemmican.

Buffalo left in 1889: 1,091. Rations became flour, sugar, coffee, bacon. Congress cut the beef ration. Then Wounded Knee. Then commodity flour, shortening, processed cheese.

Descendants today carry some of the highest diabetes rates in America, more than twice white Americans.

Same people. Same land. Same sky.

The buffalo went. The flour came. Tallest became most diabetic.

Food policy is destiny with a delay.

hits.hook: ★ 22K: Flu peaks after months of sugar; 100g sugar halves neutrophil kill power in 2h.
hits.text:
Flu season starts the same week everyone begins three straight months of eating sugar, and nobody thinks to connect the two.

31 October, the children come home with a bucket of sweets each and work through it by bedtime.

5 November brings toffee apples and bonfire toffee.

1 December, the advent calendar opens, a chocolate every morning before school for 24 days.

By mid-December there's a tin of Celebrations on every desk in every office in the country, and a selection box eaten before Christmas breakfast.

Then, around New Year, flu peaks.

In 1973 a team of researchers in California gave volunteers 100g of sugar, roughly what's in three cans of cola, and then drew their blood. They were watching the neutrophils, the white blood cells that act as your first responders and swallow bacteria whole.

Within two hours, the neutrophils' ability to swallow bacteria had fallen by about half. Five hours later it still hadn't recovered.

It made no difference whether the sugar came as table sugar, honey or orange juice. The same glass of orange juice you're handed the moment you start sniffling was in the test.

Plain starch didn't do it. Neither did going without food for 60 hours.

So we spend the darkest months knocking our first line of defence flat several times a day.

Then we blame the weather.
hits.draft_en:
Flu season peaks after three months of Halloween-to-New-Year sugar, and we blame the weather.

In 1973 California researchers gave volunteers 100 g of sugar, about three colas, then tracked neutrophils. Within two hours, bacterial killing fell by about half. Five hours later it still had not recovered. Table sugar, honey, orange juice: same hit. Plain starch did not do it. Neither did 60 hours without food.

We knock the first responders flat several times a day in the darkest months, then act shocked when the clinic fills.

Cut the sugar load before you buy another orange-juice “remedy.”

hits.hook: NEW ★ 14K: Longform lore on the $2 bill as accusation → lucky charm.
hits.text:
Once upon a time, a $2 bill in your pocket was not money. 

It was an accusation.

In early-20th-century America, the note was a walking rumor. Pull one out at a shop counter and you might as well have announced that you bet horses, bought votes, or paid for an hour you would never describe in church. Respectable people did not want the thing. Superstitious people would not keep it intact. So they tore it.

The insult started with a nickname. A two was a deuce. And “deuce,” in older English, was also a polite way to say the devil. What the deuce? meant what the devil? Carry a deuce, the folklore went, and you were carrying a scrap of hell in your wallet.

The company the bill kept did the rest.

At the racetrack, two dollars was the house unit. Churchill Downs made $2 the minimum bet in 1911, and the rest of American racing followed. 

The $2 window became the people’s window. Winners walked away with stacks of the same green paper they had risked. To a pious neighbor, a fistful of twos did not look like change. It looked like a confession.

The same number attached itself to other businesses polite society pretended not to know about. Two dollars was widely rumored to be the going rate at a cheap brothel. 

Ward bosses, in the era when votes werr the best you could  buy by the head, were said to slip a man a deuce on election day and send him to the polls. 

True in every county? Unlikely. Sticky enough to stain the denomination? Completely. A $2 bill in a wallet could be read as evidence you had gambled, sold your franchise, or come from the wrong side of town.

So Americans invented a folk vaccine.

When a deuce landed in your hand, you tore off a corner. The next owner tore another. Then another. Four tears and the jinx was spent—the devil let out through the holes. Banks of the 1920s complained that half the twos they took in arrived already mutilated, greasy, and stuck together, “a very hobo of a bill,” as the New York Times put it in 1923. 

Tellers could not push them back across the window. Customers would hit the ceiling. The only reliable exits were factory payrolls and the Treasury’s furnace. Torn corners turned legal tender into scrap.

The note never recovered its dignity in ordinary commerce. Cash registers had no slot for it. Clerks confused it with a one and shortchanged themselves. The government printed fewer of them. Scarcity, which once made the bill look shady, eventually made it look special.

That is the quiet joke of the $2 bill. The same scrap of paper Americans once ripped to keep the devil out is now tucked behind a driver’s license as a charm. 

Finding one in change feels like stumbling onto a secret. People hoard them, tip with them, press them into a grandchild’s birthday card. The curse inverted. Rarity did what superstition never could: it made the deuce lucky.

The corners, mostly, stay on.
hits.draft_en:
Once a $2 bill was not money. It was an accusation: racetrack deuce, vote grease, rumor of the wrong side of town. People tore the corners to let the “devil” out.

Scarcity flipped the curse into a charm. Same paper. New story.

Health parallel: foods and labs get moralized the same way. Reputation lags chemistry. Check the mechanism before you tear the corners off a nutrient.

hits.hook: New Sep 28: “perfect” wellness day of oats, spinach, seed oils → crash, cold feet, oxalate stack.
hits.text:
The day of eating well, by the clock.

6.45am: green smoothie. Two handfuls of spinach, half a banana, almond milk, a scoop of pea protein. The spinach alone carries more oxalate than the body can pass in a day. Nobody mentioned that in the recipe.

7.00am: overnight oats with chia, almond butter and berries. Slow release, says the blog. The oats are sugar with a delay on it. The almond butter is a jar of polyunsaturated fat, and it has been open since March.

9.30am: hungry. Confusing. She had the good breakfast. A handful of mixed nuts, for the healthy fats. More omega-6 than a chip.

10.15am: oat latte from the cart. Oats, water, rapeseed oil.

12.30pm: quinoa bowl. Roasted sweet potato, chickpeas, kale, tahini, a drizzle of dressing that is 90% sunflower oil. Three of the five things in it are on the oxalate list and the other two are the oil.

1.20pm: bloated. This is the fibre working, she has read.

3.00pm: the slump anyway. The one the cereal people get. Dark chocolate, 85%, for the antioxidants. Cocoa is the most oxalate-dense thing in the shop.

4.30pm: rice cakes and hummus. The hummus is chickpeas and rapeseed oil with a picture of an olive on it.

7.00pm: lentil dal, brown rice, spinach stirred through, roasted almonds on top. Her third spinach of the day, her fourth almond.

9.00pm: still hungry, which makes no sense on 2,100 calories of vegetables. Peanut butter on a rice cake, standing up.

11.30pm: awake. Her hands and feet are cold in a warm room. Her knee aches and she blames the running.

Six feeds, one long crash, cold feet, a knee, and a body quietly stacking oxalate crystals and rancid seed fat in the places it keeps them.

At the doctor's she is told her diet is excellent and the tiredness is probably stress.

She did everything right. The instructions were wrong.
hits.draft_en:
The day of eating “well,” by the clock.

Green smoothie with spinach oxalate overload. Overnight oats as delayed sugar. Almond butter as a jar of omega-6 open since March. Oat latte with rapeseed oil. Quinoa bowl swimming in sunflower oil. Dark chocolate for antioxidants that is oxalate-dense. Hummus with an olive on the label and seed oil in the jar. Lentil dal, more spinach, more almonds. Still hungry on 2,100 plant calories. Cold feet. Aching knee.

Doctor: diet excellent, tiredness is stress.

She followed the instructions. The instructions were wrong.

If your perfect day ends in a crash, audit oxalate and seed oils before you add another supplement.
